name: Memory FinOps Audit for Cloud SaaS
tech_why: Standard FinOps right-sizing on AWS CUR/CloudWatch, Kubernetes in-place pod resize (stable in v1.35) and Valkey migration: known techniques (TRL 9).
capital_why: T0: a read-only IAM web app plus NDA consulting audits; SOC 2 tooling fits under $50k.
ttr_why: 4-8 months (auditor set 6) to a first NDA consulting audit; the recurring subscription waits on SOC 2-style review until ~9-12 months.
usmfg_why: Pure software hosted in us-east-1; no fab dependency and no U.S. manufacturing added.
margin_why: Card 60-80% (mid 70%). Year 1 is founder-hour consulting, and only the subscription tail clears 80%.
moat_why: Free floor: AWS Compute Optimizer, Robusta KRR (MIT), VPA, Goldilocks and OpenCost. Report logic can be copied quickly.
competition_why: CAST AI, ScaleOps, StormForge, Kubecost, PerfectScale, Sedai and Densify sell this exact thing, and Intel shut down Granulate in Oct-2024 after failing to sell it.
regulatory_why: Negligible legal/export exposure. The SOC 2 gate is a commercial cost, not regulatory risk.
cycle_why: Indifferent: all 92 compared EC2 SKUs had identical prices in Sep-2025 and Oct-2026, so a DRAM glut changes nothing.
founder_why: A web app plus AWS APIs is the founder's home turf, startable part-time at T0.

name: Battery-free NV-cache / NVSRAM-replacement modules from off-the-shelf F-RAM
tech_why: TRL 9: parallel F-RAM (Infineon FM18W08/FM28V, RAMXEED MB85R8M2T 8Mbit) ships today; only per-controller (Fanuc 0i/16i/18i) card-attribute validation remains.
capital_why: T0: PCB design, an East Coast EMS run and a small parts inventory fit under $50k.
ttr_why: ~10 months (6-12) to first SKUs online and to MRO buyers; DIP drop-ins could sell sooner.
usmfg_why: U.S. EMS assembly of distribution F-RAM (Infineon die historically from TI Dallas; RAMXEED parts are Japanese): assembly, not U.S.-made memory.
margin_why: 40-55% (mid 48%) on low-volume hardware; free open-source DS1230-to-FM18W08 adapters cap DIP pricing.
moat_why: Only controller-validation know-how; the DIP niche can be copied from open designs on PCBWay/OSH Park.
competition_why: Memex sells rechargeable-battery Fanuc SRAM cards with most capacities out of stock and open adapters own DIP, but no battery-free validated PCMCIA card was found.
regulatory_why: Negligible; removing the lithium cell removes hazmat shipping.
cycle_why: Sold against batteries and failing NVSRAM, not DDR5, so it is glut-indifferent.
founder_why: PCB, firmware and a web storefront fit a hardware-adjacent software builder at a design/manufacturing day job; validation needs access to CNC controllers.

name: OpenRAM macro service for U.S. open-PDK tapeouts (SkyWater S130)
tech_why: OpenRAM v1.2.50 (2026-10-27) generates sky130 macros, but only 1-4 KB macros are published and only a 1 KB macro is silicon-verified.
capital_why: T0: ~200 hours of contract layout help plus one shuttle slot (~$9,750 per 10 mm2 in 2021) stays under $50k.
ttr_why: 9-15 months: paid generation and support can start before silicon, with characterized libraries at ~12-15 months.
usmfg_why: Customer silicon is made at SkyWater Bloomington via ChipFoundry or the Cadence/SkyWater open MPW, so the venture adds U.S.-fab ASIC capability.
margin_why: 55-75% (mid 65%), with contract layout and shuttle slots as COGS.
moat_why: The base is BSD-licensed; characterization data is a first-mover lead that UCSC, ChipFoundry or Cadence could match and bundle free.
competition_why: No paid sky130 macro vendor found; the substitutes (OpenRAM, DFFRAM) are free, and ChipFoundry runs its own marketplace.
regulatory_why: Negligible; BSD open-source tooling, EAR99.
cycle_why: Tracks MPW tapeout activity and U.S.-fab policy, not DRAM price.
founder_why: Python, CI and web work is squarely the founder's skill; tapeout support needs VLSI knowledge he must buy (~200 contract hours).

name: NVM-EOL Migration Finder (MRAM/FeRAM/ReRAM cross-reference SaaS)
tech_why: Pure software on distributor APIs and PCN feeds; TRL 9.
capital_why: T0: hosting and API access, built by the founder.
ttr_why: 6-9 months to the first paid seats.
usmfg_why: Software; no U.S. manufacturing added.
moat_why: Cross-reference tables are copyable, and Octopart/Nexar (Altium, Renesas-owned since 2024-08-01) is building lifecycle management.
competition_why: SiliconExpert (Arrow), Z2Data, Accuris, Supplyframe (Siemens) and Octopart already sell cross-reference and EOL data.
regulatory_why: Negligible; EAR99 SaaS.
cycle_why: EEPROM/NOR EOLs (Renesas last-time ship 2026-10-31) continue in a glut, but willingness to pay a 10-100x per-bit F-RAM/MRAM premium falls.
founder_why: Pure software and compatible with the day job; the risk is market size, not execution.

name: DRAM Cost & Allocation Intelligence for SMB Hardware OEMs
tech_why: Buildable on the Nexar/Octopart GraphQL, DigiKey and Mouser APIs plus free spot trackers (TRL 9).
capital_why: T0: a web app on public APIs.
ttr_why: An MVP in a few months of evenings, with 5-10 design-partner OEMs from his manufacturing network at $150-300/month; first revenue around 2Q27.
usmfg_why: Pure software; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 70-85% (mid 75%) after an allowance for an unpriced redistribution-grade data licence.
moat_why: No proprietary data. 37+ GitHub DRAM-price scrapers and the nwfella index (updated 2026-11-01) are free.
competition_why: Supplyframe Commodity IQ (Siemens) and the Counterpoint Memory Price Tracker sell the forecast layer, SiliconExpert and Z2Data own EOL, and Mobius gives its report away.
regulatory_why: Low legal risk. TrendForce/InSpectrum contract data cannot be redistributed, which limits the product rather than creating liability.
cycle_why: A shortage alert tool: buy/hold alerts are worthless at the $8.15/GB glut, and the one surviving module (EOL) belongs to SiliconExpert/Z2Data.
founder_why: Web app plus APIs, part-time, and the founder is himself a sample of the buyer.

name: CleanBOM-5949: memory-provenance verification for federal IT sellers
tech_why: SPD/JEP106 scanning is commodity (memtest86+ maps CXMT 0x0A11 and YMTC 0x091B; DDR4 bytes 350-351 give the DRAM maker), but the module-part-number-to-die-source database and lab die-ID are unproven at scale.
capital_why: T0: software plus partner-lab pass-through; no inventory or facility.
ttr_why: 9-15 months (card 12): buyers are waiting for a final FAR rule (none as of 2026-11-01), and the 2027-12-23 effective date pulls purchasing into mid/late 2027.
usmfg_why: Software and services; die-ID sampling at U.S. independent AS6171 labs; no fab dependency.
margin_why: 65-75% on software plus marked-up lab pass-through.
moat_why: The scanner is commodity code (coreboot reads DDR4 bytes 350-351; decode-dimms prints 'DRAM Manufacturer'), and SiliconExpert/Z2Data/Exiger can add a CXMT flag; only a curated die-source dataset would defend it.
competition_why: No memory-specific Sec. 5949 product was found (2026-11-01), but Exiger, Interos, Govini, SiliconExpert, Z2Data, contracts law firms and OBSIDIA ($34M CHIPS LOI, 2026-07-29) circle the niche.
regulatory_why: Revenue hinges on FAR Case 2023-008, still proposed with no final rule; its certification-after-reasonable-inquiry safe harbor already lets resellers self-attest, and a wrong attestation carries False Claims Act-adjacent liability.
cycle_why: Statute-driven (2027-12-23), not price-driven; a glut raises CXMT's share (9.5% of 2Q26 DRAM revenue) and with it the contamination risk.
founder_why: Fleet-scan tool, attestation workflow and part-number database are software the founder ships fast; the lab is outsourced, and the founder's manufacturing-ops background fits supplier attestations.

name: KV-Cache Tier Integration & Tuning for Self-Hosted LLMs
tech_why: Shipping open source: LMCache, NVIDIA Dynamo KVBM and Mooncake (in production at Kimi, integrated into vLLM/SGLang as of 2026-10-10). Integration risk only.
capital_why: T0: a ~$5-15k rented-8xH100 public benchmark is the main outlay.
ttr_why: ~12 months (9-15): benchmark, one discounted reference deployment, then a $15-40k engagement.
usmfg_why: Software and services on customers' U.S. colo GPU clusters; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 50-70% (mid 60%), services-heavy.
moat_why: Apache-2.0 components, and the recurring hit-rate/TTFT/$-per-token monitoring line is already Tensormesh's GA product.
competition_why: Tensormesh (LMCache creators, $24.5M from NVentures, AMD Ventures and CoreWeave, 2026-05-27), free NVIDIA Dynamo, WEKA, Pliops, plus Baseten/Together/Fireworks hosting.
regulatory_why: Healthcare and legal buyers self-host for data residency, so touching their clusters may need BAAs and security review. Otherwise low.
cycle_why: The value is GPU-hours avoided; a DRAM glut makes the host-DRAM tier cheaper and more attractive.
founder_why: Python/K8s skills transfer, but buyers pay for GPU-serving credibility he hasn't earned yet, in a stack that ships weekly (65 LMCache releases May-2025 to Oct-2026).

name: Memory Cost Escalation Index + EPA clause kit
tech_why: Index methodology and the Nexar/DigiKey/Mouser APIs are standard. But a list-quote index carries basis risk against contract prices, and Mobius transaction data is a hope, not a deal.
capital_why: T0: data pipeline, back-filled history, methodology and clause templates.
ttr_why: 9-15 months, and each license needs both counterparties' legal and procurement teams to accept a new index. Federal use goes case by case through pricing offices (DLAD 16.203-4).
usmfg_why: Pure software/data; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 57-89% (mid 75%). The low end applies if contract-price data must be licensed for redistribution.
moat_why: Once written into multi-year EPA clauses the index persists for the life of the contract, but TrendForce/DRAMeXchange is the default reference it has to displace.
competition_why: No memory-specific EPA index product was found, and BLS has no DRAM PPI (only PCU334413334413). TrendForce, InSpectrum, Counterpoint and Supplyframe CIQ all compete for 'reference' status.
regulatory_why: FAR 16.203-1/52.216-4 allow index-based EPA; pooled transaction data needs antitrust care, and DLAD's BLS-first rule slows federal adoption.
cycle_why: Two-sided: the 2028 −60% down-leg triggers buyer refund claims as large as the up-leg (−$105k on the card's $500k example), and embedded clauses persist. New-license sales slow only once prices go flat.
founder_why: Data pipeline, web app and contract templates are software work, startable part-time, and his manufacturing-ops job is the buyer persona. Credibility needs a procurement-lead advisory board.

name: Optane PMem Salvage: Cheap Memory-Mode Capacity for Cascade/Ice Lake Fleets
tech_why: TRL 9 parts; ipmctl health/SMART checks and burn-in are scripted.
capital_why: T0: a Cascade Lake test server (~$1-3k) plus a small inventory buy from ITADs.
ttr_why: 2-6 months to the first kits sold on eBay or a storefront.
usmfg_why: Resale and test service in an East Coast lab; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 20-35% (mid 28%): used PMem prices ($0.5-3/GB) are public on eBay.
moat_why: None: ipmctl is free, and refurb sellers (ITCreations, Uvation) already list PMem.
competition_why: Many eBay US/DE sellers plus ITADs selling lots direct; low-capital players, but a crowded market.
regulatory_why: Commercial used-parts resale; it needs only sanitization of persistent App Direct media and no sales as 'new' to federal buyers.
cycle_why: Dies twice: vSphere 8 general support ends 2027-10-11 (VCF 9 dropped PMem), and a 60% DDR4 fall in 2028-29 erases the price gap as Cascade/Ice Lake fleets retire.
founder_why: Scripting plus e-commerce, compatible with the day job; the most founder-doable card in A2.

name: Fleet Memory-Reclaim Autopilot (TMO for on-prem)
tech_why: Every piece is upstream and Meta's TMO saves 20-32% fleet-wide (ASPLOS 2022), but making swap/zswap safe across unknown customer workloads is real SLO engineering risk.
capital_why: Low T1: ~300 h of kernel-savvy contractor at $150-200/h (~$45-60k) plus test hosts pushes it just past T0.
ttr_why: ~12 months (9-15): guarded agent in 3-4 months, a 2-week volunteer-host test, then a 60-90-day paid pilot ($500-2k/month for 50-200 nodes).
usmfg_why: Pure software for fleets in U.S. colos; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 75-85% (mid 80%) per-node SaaS, after the auditor's allowance for incident support.
moat_why: It is configuration of free kernel features (zswap, Senpai-style PSI reclaim, KSM, K8s LimitedSwap). SLO guardrail data is the only know-how moat.
competition_why: No commercial on-prem reclaim product was found (MemVerge left; CAST AI and ScaleOps focus on requests), but DIY with Red Hat/Canonical tuned profiles and Proxmox KSM is the real competitor.
regulatory_why: Negligible regulatory or export exposure. Incident liability is commercial.
cycle_why: The reference fleet's deferred-DRAM value drops from ~$154k to ~$61k at -60%, and DDR4 fleets are already at ~$40-59k. Savings still beat the fee, but the urgency goes.
founder_why: The control plane is easy for him, but safe Linux-mm tuning needs a kernel contractor or cofounder, and one swap-induced outage at a pilot customer ends the company.

name: DIMM Health Subscription: predictive replacement + recovered-DDR4 spares pool
tech_why: rasdaemon logs per-DIMM CE/UE with row/page thresholds, and CE-to-UE prediction is published (IBM Research, arXiv 2212.10441, SC22), but prediction accuracy on small fleets is unproven.
capital_why: T0: 4-6 used test-bed servers plus a ~$7k spares pool per customer.
ttr_why: 6-12 months (card 9): agent and console, burn-in pool, paid pilots with 2-3 regional colo or university fleets. Universities buy slowly.
usmfg_why: U.S. burn-in of recovered RDIMMs from R2/e-Stewards ITADs, plus software; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 59% at 2026 spares prices, 82% in a glut (mid 65%).
moat_why: rasdaemon and BMC alerts are free. Only the spares pool and NBD logistics give operational stickiness.
competition_why: Park Place ParkView has bundled predictive fault detection and replacement into whole-server TPM since 2017, alongside Service Express, Dell iDRAC and HPE iLO alerts.
regulatory_why: Recovered DIMMs are fine commercially when sold as used, but FAR 52.246-26 and DFARS 252.246-7008 keep them out of federal and DoD deliverables.
cycle_why: Margin rises in a glut (spares fall from ~$4.7 to ~$1.25/GB), but demand shrinks once cheap DDR5 servers make refresh affordable and DDR4 fleets age out after ~2029.
founder_why: Agent plus console is software he ships fast, startable part-time with garage test beds. NBD shipping (~36 swaps/yr per 2,400-DIMM customer) is manageable through a 3PL.

name: Embedded RAM-Diet Profiler for Small Hardware OEMs
tech_why: Upstream and proven: smem PSS, cgroup peaks and zram (~2:1 per the kernel docs).
capital_why: T0: the contractor is paid out of per-audit fees.
ttr_why: ~12 months (9-15): recruit an embedded-Linux contractor, then sell 2-3 $5-20k audits through his manufacturing network.
usmfg_why: Software and services for U.S. industrial, IoT and medical OEMs; no manufacturing.
margin_why: 45-65% (mid 55%), because delivery is contractor labor at ~$120-180/h.
moat_why: Engineers can run smem/zram themselves for free, and nothing here is proprietary.
competition_why: No direct product. Memfault is now inside Nordic's nRF Cloud (Jun-2025), and Bootlin/Witekio-type consultancies and SoM-vendor FAEs do this ad hoc.
regulatory_why: No venture liability, but medical customers must re-validate a density step-down, which adds friction to every sale.
cycle_why: At glut prices a 1GB step saves ~$2.5/unit, below re-spin and re-qualification cost, so demand evaporates.
founder_why: His day-job network gives access, but embedded engineers rarely buy from non-engineers, and all delivery is contractor expertise.

name: TB-RAM Bare-Metal Rental from Recovered DDR4 Servers
tech_why: Plain hosting on off-lease Dell R740/HPE DL380 Gen10 boxes (TRL 9).
capital_why: The first 1.5 TB box costs ~$7.5-10.4k (24 x used 64GB at $250-370), but a viable 10-box fleet is $75-104k of peak-priced capex: low T1.
ttr_why: 4-8 months: rack 2-3 boxes in Ashburn/Secaucus colo and rent them to genomics/EDA users found via forums.
usmfg_why: Services on U.S.-sourced recovered hardware in U.S. colo; no manufacturing added.
margin_why: ~47-53% (audit11: $558-638 COGS per $1,200/month) before remote-hands fees, which a day-job operator will pay often.
moat_why: Commodity hosting with no lock-in. Tenants move on price.
competition_why: Hetzner, OVHcloud (US VA/OR), PhoenixNAP, Latitude.sh, Cherry and Vultr sell dedicated metal, and academics get free NSF ACCESS big-memory nodes. Only a cheap 1.5 TB niche is left.
regulatory_why: Low: standard hosting AUP/abuse handling, plus possible data-handling terms for genomics tenants.
cycle_why: A glut lets Hetzner/OVH restock cheaply, so a 40% rent cut drops GM to ~11-22% while 2026 DDR4 capex at $3.9-5.8/GB is stranded. Each box must pay back by end-2027.
founder_why: The portal and billing are easy and the ops background helps, but hardware failures and remote-hands on-call clash with the day job.

name: ProvenRAM: graded, serialized recovered server RDIMMs
tech_why: An existing U.S. trade (TRL 9) on free, current tools: memtest86+ (last commit 2026-10-28) and Google stressapptest (Apache-2.0).
capital_why: T0: a $20-40k start covers the test bench and the first ITAD lot.
ttr_why: 2-4 months: first ITAD lot, test bench, eBay and two B2B accounts.
usmfg_why: U.S. test-and-grade service in East Coast flex space; the value-add is testing and documentation, not manufacturing.
margin_why: 17-32% contribution in 2026 (mid ~20% after a 3-5-point inventory devaluation), and the buy side is unverified because ITADs also sell direct.
moat_why: The serialized ledger is commodity: SPD already holds an assembly serial that decode-dimms prints, and ITADs sell the same modules direct.
competition_why: ServerMonkey, Memory4Less, TechMikeNY, BuySellRAM, Curvature/Park Place, ITADs selling direct, Mobius Materials and thousands of eBay sellers.
regulatory_why: Closed to DoD (DFARS 252.246-7008), and FAR 52.246-26 treats used-as-new as counterfeit, so lot sourcing and labeling need AS6081-style discipline.
cycle_why: Resale contribution falls to ~1-6% in the glut (01_LANDSCAPE O3), and DDR4 bought at 2026-27 peak prices loses value in transit; the line must be cash-positive by end-2027.
founder_why: T0 and part-time, but the core work is lot buying, grading and shipping rather than software.

name: On-prem MoE Box (DRAM-instead-of-HBM inference appliance)
tech_why: Documented open-source configurations (KTransformers HEAD 2026-10-28: Kimi-K2.5 on >=600 GB RAM + 48 GB VRAM; DeepSeek-V4-Flash on >=200 GB + one RTX 5090). Integration only.
capital_why: Build-to-order with 50% deposits and a ~$15-20k demo unit, but each 768 GB box carries ~$15.6k of DRAM at contract (more at ~$32/GB street), so a couple of boxes in flight passes $50k: low T1.
ttr_why: 8-14 months (card 10): demo plus published benchmark, then 3-6-month security and procurement reviews at regulated buyers.
usmfg_why: Assembled and tested on an East Coast bench from TSMC CPUs/GPUs and Korean/Taiwanese DDR5: 'Assembled in USA' and TAA-compliant integration only.
margin_why: 18-25% hardware margin (the card's own BOM model gives 22%); the 60-80% subscription has no evidence of attach.
moat_why: Open-source KTransformers configs anyone can replicate; the only moat is service quality.
competition_why: Puget, Exxact, Lambda, Bizon, Supermicro and Dell Pro Max sell local-AI boxes, and NVIDIA DGX Station GB300 and 512 GB Mac Studio target the same buyer; the CPU-DRAM MoE niche for regulated SMBs has some room.
regulatory_why: Selling hardware to CMMC/ITAR subcontractors, law and healthcare firms is low-risk; only the Netlist DDR5 appliance FTO gate (01_LANDSCAPE 10.3) applies, and it is diluted by buying licensed RDIMMs.
cycle_why: A glut cuts the DRAM BOM from ~$20k to ~$8k, so the box gets cheaper and easier to sell, though gross-profit dollars per box fall with a 22% margin.
founder_why: Closest to the founder's software and ops skills and startable on deposits, but on-site support and multi-month security reviews strain a day job.

name: DRAM Continuity Vault: consignment last-time-buy storage plus LTB-sizing software
tech_why: Established practice with a standard (IEC 62435-4 nitrogen storage, J-STD-033); the LTB-sizing software uses known forecasting techniques.
capital_why: The software can start on T0, but a 2,000-4,000 sq ft ESD/climate vault, insurance and ISO 9001/AS6081 groundwork put the full service at low T1.
ttr_why: 15-18 months to the first consignment contract (card 15); paid LTB-sizing pilots could invoice at 9-12 months, but zero authorized DDR4 stock (Findchips 2026-05) stalls LTBs.
usmfg_why: U.S. services: an East Coast vault with no fab dependency.
margin_why: The card's own model is negative below ~8 OEMs, ~27% at 10 OEMs ($7.5M under management) and ~70% only at 25 OEMs in year 4+.
moat_why: Once earned, consigned OEM inventory and an AS6081-style chain-of-custody record are sticky (nobody moves $0.5-2M of critical parts lightly), but a ~$5k N2 dry cabinet caps the fee.
competition_why: Rochester (Newburyport MA), Micross, Semitron, Astute, HTV, Arrow/Avnet bonded inventory, and Super Dry/Totech DIY cabinets all serve this need.
regulatory_why: Storing customer-owned EAR99 DRAM under IEC 62435 is routine; AS6081-style custody is voluntary QA, and the main exposure is insurance and liability for held inventory.
cycle_why: Demand is EOL-driven, and a glut lets OEMs make bigger LTBs, but a ~4%/yr fee on inventory value falls as DRAM prices drop.
founder_why: The LTB-sizing software and custody ledger fit the founder and can start part-time, but the vault needs an AS6081-literate operator or partner.

name: NewSpace MRAM Radiation-Data & Upscreen Service
tech_why: Lot-level TID/SEE/proton testing is standard practice (NASA GSFC, ESA guidance); TRL 8.
capital_why: Low T1: ~$100-300k for beam time, delidded boards, a rad engineer and export compliance; each heavy-ion campaign costs ~$30-70k.
ttr_why: 18 months (15-21): TAMU/LBNL beam time is booked months ahead, and the first sale usually needs a self-funded seed dataset.
usmfg_why: U.S. test service on Everspin Chandler AZ parts at U.S. beam lines; no manufacturing added.
margin_why: A heavy-ion campaign costs ~$30-70k against $5-25k reports, and lot-specific RLAT data limits resale.
moat_why: A dataset could accumulate, but NASA NEPP and ESA ESCIES publish part-type data free, and lot-specific data resells poorly.
competition_why: Teledyne HiRel sells screened PERSYST with qualification docs from 4Q-2026; Frontgrade (QML Toggle), Honeywell 16Mb, Avalanche and TRAD R2COTS cover the rest.
regulatory_why: Certifying parts to >=500 krad TID triggers ECCN 3A001.a.1, and radiation data can be controlled technical data, which constrains sales to non-U.S. smallsat buyers.
cycle_why: Space buyers price on radiation data and heritage; DDR5 at $8.15/GB is irrelevant.
founder_why: The data platform fits the founder, but a rad-effects engineer partner is essential.

name: U.S. independent emerging-memory test and qualification lab (HZO / IGZO / AlScN)
tech_why: Routine methods (P-E loops, PUND, retention bakes, PBTI) on commercial Radiant/aixACCT testers; TRL 8.
capital_why: High T1: used tester, probe station and parametric analyzer (~$0.3-1M) plus a ~$150-180k/yr reliability engineer before utilization builds.
ttr_why: 18 months (12-24) once the engineer is hired; asset-light runs on university tools ($75-250/tool-hr) can bridge.
usmfg_why: Service lab near Albany NanoTech or Penn; no U.S. manufacturing added.
margin_why: 30-45% (mid 38%): labor-heavy at low utilization across a U.S. pool of 10-30 customers.
moat_why: The know-how sits in the hired engineer, and Radiant RT66B-class testers already sit in university shared facilities.
competition_why: No U.S. commercial specialist found (STILL-UNVERIFIED), but Neumonda/Fraunhofer IPMS abroad, Sandia and $75-250/hr university shared tools substitute.
regulatory_why: EAR99 services; only deemed-export care with foreign memory-firm customers.
cycle_why: Memory-startup funding shrinks in a glut; defense, SBIR and university demand persists.
founder_why: The founder's ops background fits running a lab, but the product is a full-time device-reliability engineer, which he is not; it cannot start part-time.

name: Supercap-Killer PLP Kit (MRAM write-cache reference design)
tech_why: The mechanism ships in IBM FCM3/4/5 MRAM journals, and Phison and Sage paired controllers with Everspin 1Gb in 2019; the kit is integration work.
capital_why: Low T1: a contract FPGA/hardware engineer (~$30-60k in year 1), boards, and $102.60 1Gb MRAM parts stay well under $500k.
ttr_why: 20 months (18-24): a 6-9-month board build, then 6-12-month OEM evaluations before a paid design-in; royalties come at 30-42 months.
usmfg_why: Reference design and IP; Everspin's 1Gb die is GF Singapore CMOS plus Chandler AZ BEOL, with U.S. CMOS only from Microchip Gresham in 2H-2027.
margin_why: 35-45% in years 1-3 because revenue is design services; 60%+ only if royalties appear.
moat_why: No IP: the kit sits between Everspin and the controller vendors (Phison, Sage, Marvell, Microchip), and Everspin could publish its own.
competition_why: No public PLP reference design found (2026-11-01), but controller vendors and IBM's in-house team gate the architecture.
regulatory_why: Single-source Everspin STT is exposed to an ITC 337-TA-1487 exclusion order (target ~Jul-2027).
cycle_why: At glut ($8.15/GB), DRAM+supercap gets ~$20-50 cheaper per board while MRAM stays ~$821/GB, so marginal designs revert.
founder_why: The founder can own drivers, test tooling and sales, but needs a contract EE for RTL and layout; slow but possible alongside the day job.

name: Legacy-DRAM buying cooperative for mid-size U.S. OEMs
tech_why: The portal is trivial software, but the core mechanism (a supplier honoring a pooled LTA from a co-op that holds neither title nor credit) has no electronics precedent (2026-11-01 search).
capital_why: The agency model needs only a portal, co-op/LC legal structuring and a memory-sales veteran: low T1. Taking title would need $8-27M (T2).
ttr_why: $10k memberships sign only after a supplier LOI exists. The 2.5% pooled-spend fee arrives with the first allocation at 12-18 months (late 2027-2028).
usmfg_why: A commercial structure with no manufacturing. It can steer pooled volume to Micron Manassas DDR4 but adds no U.S. production.
margin_why: The agency fee runs ~80-90% gross (card model: $60M pooled -> ~$1.9M revenue at ~85%).
moat_why: Member forecasts and LCs give some network lock-in, but members churn once allocation is free and nothing is exclusive.
competition_why: No electronics GPO was found, but franchised distributors (Arrow, Avnet, WPG), EMS turnkey procurement, brokers and Mobius Materials already perform the function.
regulatory_why: Joint purchasing by small OEMs with a tiny share of legacy-DRAM demand is low antitrust risk if structured properly. LC handling is routine commercial law.
cycle_why: Sells only allocation scarcity. The card says the window is ~2027 and 'gone in a glut', with fees compressing to <=1% against distributor pricing.
founder_why: The portal and operations fit, but credibility with Nanya/Winbond sales needs a memory-sales veteran cofounder.

name: U.S.-fabbed long-lifecycle SRAM second source (SkyWater Fab 25)
tech_why: Async/QDR SRAM is TRL 9 and Cypress built it at Fab 25, but whether outsiders get a characterized high-density 65nm 6T bitcell is STILL-UNVERIFIED, so expect a respin.
capital_why: T2: ~$5-15M for an SRAM design team, 65-90nm masks, a likely respin and JEDEC/AEC qualification.
ttr_why: 30-42 months: design 9-12, masks 3-4, a respin of ~6 and qualification of ~6 months before industrial orders; QML adds 12+ months.
usmfg_why: SkyWater Fab 25 Austin is an open U.S. foundry under IonQ, but whether outsiders get a characterized high-density 6T bitcell and 65nm PDK (Cypress-proprietary) is unverified.
margin_why: 45-60%: a 16Mb die costs ~$2.4 against $10-40 distributor prices.
moat_why: 15-20-year longevity commitments and DMSMS qualification lock in design-wins.
competition_why: Infineon still sells 256K-64M async/QDR SRAM from the same fab, and Renesas EOL260016 maps its 92 codes to Infineon; ISSI, GSI, Alliance and Rochester also compete.
regulatory_why: Commercial SRAM is EAR99; only the rad-tolerant 90nm option brings export/ITAR handling.
cycle_why: SRAM ASPs are decoupled from DRAM contract prices, and lifecycle buyers pay through cycles.
founder_why: Needs an SRAM design team and $5-15M from day one; the founder could only build the DMSMS demand tooling.

name: TB-Class CXL Node for EDA/Genomics/HANA
tech_why: Samsung CMM-D, Micron CZ122 and SK hynix CMM ship; weighted interleave (Linux v6.9) and DAMON tiering (v6.11) are upstream. Integration risk only.
capital_why: Two validated reference configs with 2-4 TB of CXL plus local DDR5 tie up roughly $100-200k each at ~$20-26/GB: high T1.
ttr_why: 12-18 months (card 15): two reference configs, then a first sale through EDA/genomics channels against OEM incumbents.
usmfg_why: U.S. integration of Korean CMM modules and imported servers.
margin_why: 15-25% VAR margin (mid 20%) against OEMs selling the same modules.
moat_why: CXL modules are merchant parts and tiering is free upstream software (HMSDK, SMDK), so anyone with a server can copy it.
competition_why: Penguin CXL expansion servers, Supermicro, Dell, HPE, Lenovo, Colfax, Silicon Mechanics and cloud high-memory instances already serve these buyers.
regulatory_why: Commodity servers to EDA/genomics/HANA buyers: no export, counterfeit or patent gate.
cycle_why: In a glut, 128-256 GB RDIMMs give ~3-6 TB per socket without CXL, so only jobs above the slot ceiling still need the node; the revenue line shrinks hard.
founder_why: Linux tiering is learnable, but EDA, genomics and HANA buyers purchase from OEMs they already trust, so it needs an infrastructure-sales partner and is hard to run part-time.

name: AS6171 counterfeit-detection and authentication lab for memory lots
tech_why: AS6171 visual, X-ray, XRF, decap and electrical memory test are routine (TRL 9).
capital_why: High T1: $650k capex plus $478k/yr fixed cost, and losses until 36 lots/month, so ~$1-1.5M before breakeven.
ttr_why: 12-18 months (card 15) for equipment, quality system, proficiency tests and the ANAB 17025/AS6171 scope assessment before defense buyers send lots.
usmfg_why: U.S. lab services; no manufacturing.
margin_why: Mid 22% at 40 lots/month, -34% at 20, and 41% only at 60 lots/month (1.7x breakeven).
moat_why: 17025/AS6171 accreditation is table stakes that every competitor holds, and die-origin flagging uses the same decap/die-marking methods.
competition_why: SMT Corp (Sandy Hook CT, AS6171 HRL2, DLA QTSL) sits in the target corridor. Micross Clearwater runs full-lot AS6171 with a RAM tester in ~2 weeks, and A2 Global, Vyrian and White Horse Labs also compete.
regulatory_why: ITAR registration for defense lots and liability for a false pass are manageable under DFARS 252.246-7008/AS6171.
cycle_why: Broker lots fall ~30-50% when authorized stock returns. Against $478k/yr fixed cost and a 36-lot/month breakeven, that pushes the lab back into losses.
founder_why: LIMS and serialized reports are his, but accreditation requires a hired AS6171 test engineer and an operating lab from day one, which doesn't fit a day job.

name: KV Pool Node (shared DRAM+CXL KV-cache appliance)
tech_why: All parts are off the shelf and the stack is in production (Mooncake at Kimi, 75% more requests within SLO; LMCache /dev/dax); Penguin already ships the identical box. Integration risk only.
capital_why: A 4 TB node ties up ~$80-130k of DRAM at 4Q26 prices and unknown integrators won't get prepayment, so a demo plus the first 2-3 orders needs ~$0.5M [ESTIMATE].
ttr_why: 12-18 months (card 15): a demo node, then 1-2 design wins against Penguin MemoryAI and OEM reference boxes.
usmfg_why: U.S. integration and burn-in of imported CPUs, NICs, DDR5 and CXL modules (Micron Idaho DDR5 not before mid-2027).
margin_why: 10-20% hardware margin while buying the key CXL AIC from Penguin/SMART, a vertically integrated competitor; the subscription attach is unproven.
moat_why: A commodity server plus open-source Mooncake/LMCache that OEM reference designs replicate; there is nothing to own.
competition_why: Penguin MemoryAI launched 2026-03-16 (3 TB DDR5 + 8x1 TB CXL), and NVIDIA BlueField-4 ICMS/CMX ships 2H26 via Dell, HPE, IBM, VAST, WEKA, DDN, Pure and Supermicro.
regulatory_why: Commodity server integration from authorized channels for domestic buyers: no export, counterfeit or module-patent exposure.
cycle_why: A glut cuts the node BOM but stretches DRAM break-even reuse from 1.35 h to 3.4 h, and it lets every OEM sell the same box; flash tiers keep undercutting warm KV.
founder_why: Software integration is reachable, but ~$100k DRAM working capital per node and the GPU-infrastructure credibility neocloud buyers demand rule out a part-time start.

name: Si gain-cell eDRAM (GCRAM) IP for U.S. trailing-node SoCs
tech_why: Si gain cells are silicon-proven (RAAAM, 180nm-5nm), but GF's own GCRAM is only a 2026 test vehicle, 85-125C retention of ~10-100 us forces refresh, and this venture's S130 macro does not exist (TRL 5).
capital_why: T2: ~$2-5M for a memory-circuit team, two MPW spins and an FTO opinion.
ttr_why: 36 months (30-42): 6-9 mo of design plus two ~6-month SkyWater MPW turns before a paid evaluation license.
usmfg_why: Targets SkyWater S130/S90 and GF 12LP+ Malta, with U.S. MPW test chips (ChipFoundry, Cadence/SkyWater).
margin_why: 80-90% on a zero-extra-mask license and royalty.
moat_why: Own patents are possible, but the RAAAM/Bar-Ilan/EPFL estate is an FTO gate for an entrant with no silicon.
competition_why: RAAAM ($17.5M Series A led by NXP, GF FDX test vehicle, TSMC 2nm qualification) can port to S130 at will; Synopsys and Arm own SRAM compilers.
regulatory_why: IP licensing; trusted-ASIC customers add only routine handling.
cycle_why: Priced in SoC die area, decoupled from DDR5.
founder_why: The founder could build the compiler automation and portal, but needs a full-time memory-circuit cofounder and an FTO opinion before that matters.

name: Rugged and new-form-factor memory modules built at a U.S. EMS (LPCAMM2/CAMM2, wide-temp coated SODIMM)
tech_why: Shipping category (TRL 9): Innodisk launched screw-lock DDR5/LPDDR5X CAMM2 in Aug-2025, and congatec ships a -40 to +85 C LPCAMM2 module (Apr-2026).
capital_why: High T1: raw-card design, environmental qualification and EMS NRE, plus die inventory at ~$20/GB contract. 1,000 x 16GB modules is ~$320k of DRAM alone.
ttr_why: ~24 months (18-30): allocation agreement, then a 12-24-month design-win cycle while authorized Micron DDR4 stock sits at zero (Findchips, May-2026).
usmfg_why: U.S. EMS assembly of imported die. Even Manassas DDR4 die is packaged in Malaysia/India, and DDR5/LPDDR5X SKUs carry only Asian die.
margin_why: 20-35% now (mid 25%) and 10-27% in the glut, per the card.
moat_why: Some qualified-BOM stickiness at rugged-computer makers, but the module is a commodity that Virtium, ATP or Innodisk can match.
competition_why: Virtium, SMART (Penguin), ATP, Swissbit, Cervoz and Innodisk already serve rugged buyers, and Micron, Samsung and SK hynix make CAMM-class modules themselves.
regulatory_why: Rugged commercial modules are mostly EAR99; the burden is counterfeit-avoidance die sourcing for defense buyers (DFARS 252.246-7008).
cycle_why: Module price tracks DRAM down, so dollar margin shrinks ~55% and GM falls to 10-27%. That leaves little room on top of a fixed EMS and qualification cost base.
founder_why: The founder's product-dev and manufacturing-ops day job is relevant, but an SI/hardware cofounder and an EMS partner are required, and it is not a part-time start.

name: Analog CIM Edge Module (DRAM-free defense edge inference)
tech_why: Mythic M1076 (25 TOPS at ~3 W, weights on-chip) has shipped, including to Lockheed Martin; the venture's work is ruggedization and environmental qualification of a shipping chip.
capital_why: T1: rugged M.2/PCIe NRE, MIL-STD-style environmental qualification and vendor MOQs before a paid defense pilot, ~$0.5-1M [ESTIMATE].
ttr_why: 18-30 months (card 24): vendor partnership, ruggedized module, then an SBIR or defense pilot.
usmfg_why: U.S.-designed chips (Mythic Austin, EnCharge Santa Clara) fabbed offshore, with module assembly and environmental test at a U.S. EMS.
margin_why: 25-40%: a defense rugged-module premium, capped by channel conflict because Mythic and EnCharge sell their own M.2/PCIe cards.
moat_why: The only moat is environmental qualification and program design-ins, which Curtiss-Wright, Mercury and Aitech already hold.
competition_why: Edge AI for UAS/ISR is dominated by NVIDIA Jetson, Qualcomm and Hailo-8 (DRAM-free M.2), plus chip vendors selling modules direct; only the analog-CIM rugged niche is open.
regulatory_why: Defense UAS/ISR buyers bring CMMC Level 2, possible ITAR registration and drone-component sourcing rules: manageable but real.
cycle_why: The axis is W per inference on U.S.-designed silicon, which does not depend on DRAM price; the glut only weakens the secondary 'avoid +70-90% LPDDR' argument.
founder_why: Needs an EE for rugged board and thermal design plus defense BD, and the SBIR PI rule excludes a founder who keeps a day job.

name: Authorized-aftermarket die bank for EOL legacy DRAM (title-taking LTB aggregator)
tech_why: The model is proven at scale: Rochester's wafer bank (>10B die, expanding to ~30B) and Micross authorized die.
capital_why: T2: ~$0.6M of LTB wafers per part and $2M+ for a portfolio, plus an AS9120/AS6496 quality system.
ttr_why: 6-18 months to an OCM authorization no startup has been shown to win, then the card's own curve sells 90% of the bank in years 3-8. Realistically more than 36 months.
usmfg_why: Taiwanese Winbond/ESMT/Etron/Nanya die banked, packaged and tested at U.S. OSATs (Micross Apopka FL, QP Technologies, Integra KS).
margin_why: 33-66% unit GM (mid 50%), with a bear-case -7% IRR from banked die that never sells.
moat_why: DFARS 252.246-7008 and 246.870-2 rank authorized aftermarket manufacturers ahead of independents, a genuine regulatory moat, but only if an OCM grants the authorization.
competition_why: Rochester (Newburyport MA, 70+ OCM authorizations, legacy DRAM via Intelligent Memory), Micross, Intelligent Memory, Alliance Memory and Micron Manassas long-lifecycle DDR4.
regulatory_why: AS9120/AS6496 quality systems and defense customer flow-downs are manageable but heavy compliance.
cycle_why: EOL-driven demand persists, but LTB wafers bought at repriced 2026-27 levels (Nanya LTAs +60%) sell into a glut that lowers the independent-market price cap.
founder_why: Needs OCM relationships, a quality system and $2M+ of inventory capital, with a full-time team. No software leverage at all.

name: Compute-in-SRAM vector-search appliance on GSI Gemini APU
tech_why: Gemini APU ships (TRL 7) and GSI already sells production Gemini-I servers; the venture's FAISS/Milvus API layer is known-technique software, so the risk is integration plus vendor survival.
capital_why: Card puts eval hardware and pilots at ~$100-300k, which is low T1 (<$500k); it is not reachable on the founder's <$50k.
ttr_why: 21 months (18-24): a first air-gapped defense/IC pilot needs a prime sponsor and an ATO, and GSI's own vector-search sales have not converted since 2021.
usmfg_why: APU silicon is TSMC 28/16nm and boards are GSI-sourced; only integration and software are U.S., so this is U.S. assembly of imported silicon.
margin_why: Blended 20-40%, but years 1-2 are dominated by card/server resale at a ~10-20% VAR margin from a vendor that sells the same boxes direct.
moat_why: GSI has sold the same Gemini-I servers and an OpenSearch k-NN plugin since 2021, so the founder's layer competes with the vendor's own product.
competition_why: Vector search is crowded with funded players (NVIDIA cuVS/CAGRA, Milvus/Zilliz, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone) plus GSI selling direct; only the air-gapped APU niche is thin.
regulatory_why: Defense/IC buyers need an ATO and likely CMMC Level 2 (~$30-100k first year, Phase 2 from ~2026-11-10); manageable, with no export problem in the domestic market.
cycle_why: The energy pitch (54-118x below an A6000, MICRO '25, GSI co-authored) does not depend on DRAM price, but GSI (Q1 FY2027 operating loss $5.4M) is weaker if its SRAM base shrinks in a downturn.
founder_why: The software stack is in the founder's wheelhouse, but defense/IC selling needs a cleared BD partner and a prime sponsor, which a part-time founder lacks.

name: U.S. hi-rel DDR4/LPDDR4 multi-chip memory design house
tech_why: Hi-rel x72 DDR4 MCMs ship (Teledyne e2v DDR4T04G72 since 2020), but an entrant's Winbond/ESMT KGD has no radiation or -55 to 125 C characterization, so qualification can still fail.
capital_why: T2: ~$2-4M of package/SI engineering, environmental and radiation qualification before the first design-in (card founder note).
ttr_why: 30-42 months (card 36): substrate SI/PI 6-9 mo, qualification 6-12 mo, then a design-in against parts with six years of flight heritage.
usmfg_why: Die is <15% of ASP (~$457 unit cost vs $800-3,000), and design, assembly, screening and qualification happen at U.S. OSATs that take outside work (Micross Apopka FL, QP Technologies, Integra Wichita).
margin_why: The card's mid is 60%, but an entrant has to undercut Teledyne e2v and sits near the $800 end: $457 cost gives ~43%.
moat_why: A won hi-rel design-in locks in for 10-20 years, but the entrant has no heritage to win it with, so the moat is only potential.
competition_why: The exact flagship SKU already ships from Teledyne e2v, and Micross, Mercury, DDC, Frontgrade and 3D Plus (HEICO) all hold flight and field heritage. Micross is also the die and OSAT supplier.
regulatory_why: Defense and space buyers bring ITAR/EAR handling and DFARS 252.246-7008 traceability. Manageable, but real paperwork.
cycle_why: Priced on qualification and heritage, not bits. But the 'cheaper non-Level-1' niche competes with upscreened COTS DDR4, which gets cheaper at the $8.15/GB glut.
founder_why: Needs package/SI engineers, defense BD and $2-4M full-time from day one (card: 'doable_by_founder: no'). Nothing here is web-app work.

name: TrustNVM: U.S.-Made ReRAM Secure-NVM Chiplet on SkyWater S130
tech_why: Weebit ReRAM is qualified in S130 at 256Kb (3 lots, 125C), but a 1-4Mb product needs new macros and requalification, and the rad claim rests on 16-kbit gamma-only tests (TRL 3-4).
capital_why: ~$1.5-3M+: two MPWs ($30-120k), production masks (~$0.5-0.6M), qualification lots ($0.3-0.5M), 2-3 years of IC designer, plus a Weebit fee (its first-ever fee was $100k).
ttr_why: Design 6-9 mo, MPW 4-6 mo, a production run, 12-18 mo qualification (Weebit's own 2026-07 figure), then defense design-in: real revenue lands past 36 months, and SBIR does not count.
usmfg_why: SkyWater Bloomington S130 (open foundry under IonQ since 2026-07-31, DMEA trusted) has ReRAM in the PDK, with U.S. OSATs (Integra, Promex).
margin_why: 50-65% on $20-200 defense part ASPs after the Weebit royalty.
moat_why: Defense design-wins lock in for 15-20 years, but the Weebit license is non-exclusive and SkyWater can sell the same module to anyone.
competition_why: Weebit's first U.S. security licensee may already own this slot; Everspin Toggle (16-32Mb, $40M DoW onshore program), Honeywell trusted MRAM and Microchip EEPROM compete.
regulatory_why: Trusted-flow defense parts bring ITAR/EAR handling, and the rad variant falls under 3A001.a.1.
cycle_why: Defense trusted-NVM demand is decoupled from DRAM price.
founder_why: Founder can be CEO/BD, but needs a mixed-signal IC designer cofounder and SBIR money (the SBIR PI rule excludes him while he keeps his day job).

name: Persistent CXL Log Card (post-Optane PMem for WAL/journals)
tech_why: NVDIMM-N is TRL 9, and SMART/Penguin's NV-CMM (CXL 2.0, DRAM+NAND+energy source) passed CXL compliance in 2026-01; an entrant re-implements it with power-fail firmware risk.
capital_why: T2: card design, power-fail firmware and CXL compliance (12-18 months), then OEM qualification.
ttr_why: 30-42 months (card 36): SMART needed ~10 months from sampling to compliance alone, and storage/DB OEM design-ins take another 12-24 months.
usmfg_why: U.S. board assembly; the Toggle MRAM variant can use Everspin Chandler AZ parts, but DRAM, NAND and the controller are imported.
margin_why: 25-40% (mid 30%): DRAM dominates the BOM and an incumbent with Tier-1 OEM channels sets the persistence premium.
moat_why: Power-fail firmware know-how is real, but the qualification lock-in that would be the moat already belongs to SMART at Tier-1 OEMs.
competition_why: SMART/Penguin NV-CMM (sampling since 2025-03, Integrators List 2026-01), Samsung CMM-H, Kioxia XL-Flash, and in-house OEM journals (IBM FlashCore MRAM since 2018).
regulatory_why: The MRAM variant inherits ITC 337-TA-1487 (Avalanche v. Everspin, target ~2027-07) exposure, and NVDIMM-style backup has a litigated patent history.
cycle_why: Value is persistence, not $/GB, so demand holds in a glut; the BOM (and likely the ASP) falls from ~$1.3k to ~$0.5k per 64 GB card for incumbent and entrant alike.
founder_why: Needs power-fail firmware, CXL compliance and storage-OEM qualification engineers full-time; the founder's software speed is secondary.

name: AlScN ferro-diode memory for 500-600C electronics (Penn/AFRL license + STTR)
tech_why: Diodes switch at 600C for >60 h (Nature Electronics 2024) and kB crossbars exist only as a preprint (arXiv 2506.05452), but 500C periphery (SiC CMOS/JFET) is lab/program-only and drive is 10-15 V.
capital_why: T1 via a Penn option plus STTR (Phase I ~$323k, Phase II ~$2.15M): ~$1-2.5M, mostly grant money, before eval-part sales.
ttr_why: 42 months (36-48); AF254-D0806 and DV017 are both closed, and STTR money is funding, not revenue (A-04).
usmfg_why: Prototyping at Penn Singh Center (open to industry, $75-250/tool-hr) and U.S. high-temperature ceramic packaging; which U.S. foundry offers AlScN to outsiders at volume is unverified.
margin_why: 40-60% on small eval lots dominated by fab-lot and high-temperature packaging cost; Phase III work is often cost-plus.
moat_why: An exclusive Penn/AFRL license would be a real moat, but no license or spin-out was found in two 2026-11 searches.
competition_why: No incumbent RAM or flash works at 500C+; the risk is the unknown AF254-D0806 scale-up performer, who may already hold the seat.
regulatory_why: Hypersonic and engine buyers bring 3A001/9A515 or ITAR XV(d) plus deemed-export rules; manageable because the core buyer is U.S. DoD.
cycle_why: Completely decoupled from DDR5; a 60% glut changes nothing for 500C electronics.
founder_why: STTR lets the founder start part-time as CEO/BD with a Penn PI for <$50k, but a device CTO is required and revenue lands past 36 months.

name: U.S.-made HZO FeRAM family (1-16 Mb, rad-hard option) via SkyWater + Sandia
tech_why: 1Mb HZO 1T1C arrays exist (IEDM 2023) and Sandia put HZO FeRAM in its 200mm MESA fab (2026-05), but research arrays reach ~1e11 cycles and 10 yr at 85C, against PZT's 1e13-1e14 cycles and 10 yr at 125C.
capital_why: T2: an HZO module at SkyWater plus a memory design and reliability team, ~$10-30M before the first sale.
ttr_why: 54 months (42-72) to first industrial/eval sales; QML-V for the space buyer adds another 1-2 years.
usmfg_why: No HZO module at SkyWater S130 or Fab 25; Sandia MESA access is CRADA-limited and its FeRAM circuitry is still a planned follow-on.
margin_why: 50-65% (mid 58%) on high-rel ASPs, on very low volumes.
moat_why: QML qualification lock-in would be real once achieved; the Sandia license is unconfirmed (no listing or CRADA offer found).
competition_why: Infineon owns QML-V 2Mb F-RAM and its Excelon die is already U.S.-fabbed (TI Dallas DMOS6); RAMXEED runs its own HZO R&D, CEA-Leti has 22nm eFeRAM, and U.S.-made Everspin toggle MRAM already serves space.
regulatory_why: Rad-hard variants fall under 3A001.a.1/9A515 or ITAR XV(d); manageable for a U.S.-defense core market at ~$25-75k/yr compliance.
cycle_why: Mb-class NVM priced on reliability and supply security; DDR5 at $8.15/GB is irrelevant to a part costing ~$814/GB.
founder_why: Needs a memory designer, a reliability engineer and $10-30M; the card itself rates founder-doability 'no'.

name: DDR4 Second-Life CXL Expander
tech_why: TRL 7: the Marvell Structera X 2404 (12 DDR4-3200 DIMMs at 3 DPC) has only sampled since Q4 2024, and signal integrity and qualification of mixed used DIMMs at 3 DPC are unproven for a small vendor.
capital_why: T2 ($2M+): board design, controller access, firmware/SI team and CXL compliance before the first tier-2 qualification.
ttr_why: 24 months (18-30): board, controller-vendor access and qualification at one tier-2 cloud.
usmfg_why: Board assembly at a U.S. EMS (Sanmina) and DIMMs recovered from U.S. data centers, but the controller silicon is TSMC: U.S. assembly of imported silicon.
margin_why: 15-30% on the card (mid 22%), i.e. ~$270-540 of gross profit per ~$1.8k card; it needs thousands of cards a year.
moat_why: A qualified mixed-DIMM compatibility matrix would be know-how, but there is no IP, and controller allocation sits with Marvell's hyperscaler accounts.
competition_why: No GA DDR4-reuse CXL card sold to tier-2 operators was found; Penguin/SMART CXL AICs and hyperscaler in-house reuse (Microsoft/Meta) are adjacent.
regulatory_why: The owner's own recovered DIMMs in a commercial card: no counterfeit or DFARS exposure, and the Netlist DDR5-PMIC gate does not apply to DDR4 reuse.
cycle_why: Reuse still saves ~$4.3-5.3/GB at the ~$8.1/GB glut deck but loses $0.3-0.8/GB at a 2023-style trough, and freed DDR5 allocation shrinks volume.
founder_why: Needs controller-vendor access, a full-time board/firmware/SI team and $2M+; the founder's software edge barely applies.

name: OS-eDRAM: IGZO/IWO 2T0C gain-cell memory IP on a U.S. 200mm foundry
tech_why: TRL 4: imec 2T0C cells (IEDM 2020/21) only; PBTI reaches 5-yr at 95C in lab (IEDM 2025 snippet), no 10-yr lifetime, and IWO retention falls to ~300 ms at 85C.
capital_why: T2: dedicated IGZO/In2O3 BEOL tools ($4-10M) plus ~$10-30M module qualification at SkyWater before any NRE or royalty.
ttr_why: 48 months (36-60): 18-24 mo module development plus 12-18 mo PBTI/retention qualification before first NRE, past the 36-month hard ceiling.
usmfg_why: No oxide-semiconductor module exists at SkyWater Bloomington or Fab 25 (2026-11 search), so it needs U.S. capacity that does not exist yet.
margin_why: Card says 65-85% blended, but early revenue is NRE/test-chip support and the foundry captures the wafer adder, so the early band is about 50-70%.
moat_why: A qualified foundry module would be sticky, but SEL's dominant oxide-semiconductor patent estate is an FTO risk and no Georgia Tech/Notre Dame/Purdue license is secured.
competition_why: No commercial oxide eDRAM at a U.S. foundry, but live substitutes exist: Weebit ReRAM qualified in S130 and RAAAM's Si gain cell (C-32), which needs no new module.
regulatory_why: Mostly EAR99-class IP licensing to edge-AI ASIC teams; DoD sensor-ASIC buyers add only routine compliance.
cycle_why: Priced against on-die SRAM/ReRAM, not DDR5; DDR5 at $8.15/GB does not change an ASIC's on-die memory choice.
founder_why: Process-module development and reliability qualification need a device/process CTO and a SkyWater JDA from day one; the founder only adds a compiler GUI or data portal.

name: eMRAM-Unified-Memory Edge MCU (no external DRAM)
tech_why: Foundry eMRAM ships (GF AutoPro150 on 22FDX; Renesas RA8P1 with 1MB on TSMC 22ULL), but a 128-512Mb macro on 22FDX has not been shown.
capital_why: T2 fabless SoC: 22nm mask sets, an SoC team and AEC qualification cost tens of $M.
ttr_why: 48 months: SoC design, AEC/industrial qualification and an ecosystem.
usmfg_why: GF 22FDX eMRAM is made in Dresden and TSMC RRAM in Taiwan; no U.S. line offers 22nm eNVM.
margin_why: 40-55% (mid 45%) against Renesas/ST pricing power.
moat_why: MCU design-wins are sticky, but a startup has no ecosystem, and the only differentiator (16-64MB on-die) is die area anyone can buy.
competition_why: Renesas RA8P1, Infineon PSoC Edge (RRAM), ST STM32V8 (ePCM), SEMIFIVE/ICY Tech on Samsung 8nm eMRAM and Everspin UNISYST already do exactly this.
regulatory_why: EAR99 MCU; automotive functional-safety qualification is the main burden.
cycle_why: Launch (~2030) lands in the glut, when 512MB LPDDR4X falls from ~$10.5 to ~$4 and the 'no external DRAM' BOM pitch collapses.
founder_why: A full SoC company; the founder has no critical-path role.

name: U.S.-fabbed SRAM-only LLM inference accelerator (Groq pattern)
tech_why: The SRAM-only decode pattern ships at Groq (TRL 9, Llama-2 70B at 240 tok/s/user), but a new GF 12LP+ chip plus compiler is a full silicon program, not integration.
capital_why: The minimum path is ~$150-400M to first rack revenue (T3; Groq raised ~$300M by 2021, d-Matrix $110M+ in 2023).
ttr_why: 48-60 months: ~24-30 months to first silicon, then the compiler and rack integration; Groq took 4+ years to meaningful revenue.
usmfg_why: Wafers could come from GF Fab 8 Malta NY (open foundry, Trusted), but U.S. flip-chip packaging of large dies for outside customers is thin (Amkor AZ not before ~2028).
margin_why: The card gives 20-50% even for a winner; a 12LP+ entrant that gives up 2-3x SRAM density and needs ~300+ dies per 70B 8-bit model sits at the low end, against GPU-cloud token prices.
moat_why: Any chip IP would be the venture's own, but NVIDIA took a non-exclusive license to Groq's inference tech (~$20B, 2025-12-24), and 'U.S.-fabbed' is not unique.
competition_why: Groq, NVIDIA (Groq license plus its founder), Cerebras, d-Matrix, SambaNova, Etched, MatX and Positron are all well funded and doing exactly this.
regulatory_why: AI accelerators fall under BIS advanced-computing controls (3A090/4A090), which close export markets; the U.S. market is open and Section 232's 25% on imported accelerators slightly helps.
cycle_why: A glut means cheaper HBM, which inverts the SRAM cost story (~30x HBM-class $/GB), and the 2028-29 glut assumes slowing AI capex, which starves accelerator funding.
founder_why: A $100M+ chip company that needs a veteran silicon, compiler and systems team full-time from day one.

name: Compressed CXL Expander (licensed inline compression IP)
tech_why: Inline compression is in merchant silicon (Structera X 4x LZ4, sampling Q4 2024; DenseMem in TSMC 5nm), but the venture's own FPGA CXL card is TRL 5-6 per the auditor.
capital_why: T2: a ZeroPoint license fee plus Agilex 7 R-tile / Versal Premium cards, RTL and CXL compliance work before any operator qualification.
ttr_why: 30-42 months (card 36): ZeroPoint states 24-36-month sales cycles before the FPGA card and operator qualification even start.
usmfg_why: The FPGA is TSMC and the IP is from Sweden; only board assembly at a U.S. EMS is domestic.
margin_why: 20-40%, and an FPGA card with a $3-8k BOM cannot price at the full ~$10.4k DRAM saving when Structera-based ASIC cards exist.
moat_why: The compression IP is licensed non-exclusively (ZeroPoint sells to SoC makers), so the venture is a downstream FPGA integrator of IP its competitors put into cheaper ASICs.
competition_why: Marvell Structera X, ZeroPoint's licensee (a 'major global semiconductor manufacturer', 2024-03), free Intel IAA + zswap and Meta TMO cover the job; only the GA mid-market card is unserved.
regulatory_why: A domestic FPGA card with licensed IP: no DoD sourcing, PMIC or export exposure in the core market.
cycle_why: Glut kills it: at the ~$8.1/GB RDIMM deck, 2x on 512 GB saves ~$4.2k, which no longer covers a $3-8k FPGA card plus the latency penalty.
founder_why: Needs a full-time RTL/FPGA team, CXL compliance expertise and a later ASIC tape-out; nothing about it is a part-time software job.

name: LPDDR 'HBM-lite' Memory Chiplet (UCIe/AIB-attached)
tech_why: TRL 5: UCIe/AIB and LPDDR5X PHY IP are commercial and Grace proves 512-bit LPDDR5X (~546 GB/s), but a merchant LPDDR chiplet behind UCIe has never been built.
capital_why: T3: a ~$50-90M program for architecture, tape-out, package qualification and the first design-in.
ttr_why: 36-48 months (card 42) to the first design-in revenue.
usmfg_why: GF Malta could fab the controller die, but Amkor Peoria AZ is anchor-customer-only (production ~early 2028), so packaging and LPDDR5X dies are offshore in practice.
margin_why: 40-60% for a sub-scale chiplet seller that carries package and test cost and competes with IP royalties.
moat_why: Own chiplet design IP and design-in lock-in are possible, but Synopsys, Cadence and Alphawave license the LPDDR5X controller/PHY to any ASIC team directly.
competition_why: IP giants (Synopsys, Cadence, Alphawave), Eliyan and Marvell, plus buyers that integrate LPDDR directly (Qualcomm AI200, d-Matrix Corsair, NVIDIA Grace).
regulatory_why: AI-memory chiplets sit near BIS HBM/advanced-computing controls for export, and defense ASIC programs add trusted-sourcing requirements; manageable domestically.
cycle_why: A glut eases HBM allocation and removes the core 'can't get HBM' motive; only a residual LPDDR $/GB cost niche remains.
founder_why: A T3 silicon program that needs a veteran SoC, PHY and packaging team from day one.
